Digital Safety Councils -- Idea for a Protocol

Spend time with folks in their golden years, and you quickly realize digital safety is a real thing. There's a lot of scams and scurrilous activity out on the nets. Consider the following from Harpers magazine's amazing Index:

> Portion of Democratic small-dollar donations given by Americans aged 65 or older in response to harassing texts or emails : 1/2
November 2026 • Source: Adam Bonica, Stanford University (Calif.)

> Average number of times such donors have given money during this year’s election cycle : 156
November 2026 • Source: Adam Bonica, Stanford University (Calif.)

> Estimated number of small-dollar donors who have donated more than one hundred times since 2017 : 138000
November 2026 • Source: Adam Bonica, Stanford University (Calif.)

[Many towns and counties have a fire safety council. It's usually a loose, mostly volunteer group: someone from the fire department, a few neighbors, a school representative, a local business owner, sometimes an insurance agent or a landlord. They don't fight fires. Their job is to keep fires from happening, and to make sure people know what to do when one does. They check that smoke alarms work and install them in homes that lack them, run a fire drill at the elementary school, hand out checklists, and talk to seniors about space heaters and kitchen habits. Once a year they hold an awareness week with a lot of pamphlets and a fire truck for the kids.

Three things about that model are worth borrowing.

**The threat is shared, and so is the response.** Nobody expects a single household to engineer its own fire code. The community agrees on a baseline (working alarms, clear exits, a practiced plan) and helps everyone reach it, especially people who can't easily do it themselves.

**Prevention is local and personal.** The council doesn't send a form letter. A person who knows your street comes to your door, looks at your actual kitchen, and tells you what to fix. That trust is why it works.

**Professionals are connected to the neighborhood.** The fire department supplies expertise, but the council supplies reach: the church bulletin, the senior center, the block captain who knows which neighbor lives alone.

Now swap the threat. The scam texts, fake invoices, "your account has been locked" emails, and relentless fundraising pitches in the numbers above are the digital equivalent of faulty wiring in an old house. Most people can't inspect it themselves, and the people who exploit it count on that.

A digital safety council would work the same way. A handful of neighbors, a librarian, someone from the credit union, a retired IT worker, a teenager who's good with phones, and maybe a local police liaison could agree on a baseline and help people meet it. Instead of smoke alarms, the baseline might be two-factor authentication, a trusted person to call before sending money, a habit of never acting on a message that creates urgency, and unsubscribe and blocking tools set up on the phone. They could run "digital drills" too, such as a mock scam call at the senior center, so the first time someone hears a panicked voice demanding gift cards isn't the real time.

The point is the protocol, not the particulars: a standing group, a shared baseline, in-person help, and a clear path to professionals when something goes wrong. We already know how to organize around fire. The same instinct could be pointed at what's coming through the phone.]
